target: Bom final de semana!
tip: Brazilians say 'final de semana' for weekend; 'fim de semana' is more common in Portugal. Both are correct.

target: Está tudo bem sim, obrigado.
tip: 'Obrigado' agrees with the speaker's gender: a man says 'obrigado', a woman says 'obrigada', regardless of who they thank.

target: Beleza, a gente se vê amanhã.
tip: 'Beleza' means 'beauty' but is used as 'okay/cool/deal.' 'Beleza?' can also be a greeting: 'E aí, beleza?' = Hey, what's up?

target: Tudo bem com você?
tip: 'Tudo bem' is the most common greeting in Brazil. You can answer with 'tudo bem,' 'tudo ótimo,' or just 'tudo.'

target: Imagina, não foi nada.
tip: 'Imagina' is how Brazilians casually say 'don't mention it' or 'no worries.' Used when someone thanks you or apologizes.

target: Boa sorte na prova!
tip: 'Prova' here means a test or exam, not 'proof'. Common in school contexts: prova final, prova de matemática.

target: Mentira! Não é possível.
tip: 'Mentira' literally means 'lie', but shouted on its own it works as 'no way' or 'you're kidding'.

target: Vocês gostaram do restaurante?
tip: gostar always needs de before the thing you like: gostaram do restaurante (liked the restaurant), never gostar it directly.

target: O chefe é bastante exigente.
tip: 'Bastante' before an adjective means 'quite' or 'pretty': 'bastante exigente' = quite demanding.

target: A situação é complicada demais.
tip: 'Demais' after an adjective means 'too much': 'complicada demais' = too complicated. It's very common in Brazilian Portuguese.

target: Ele ficou vermelho de vergonha.
tip: 'Ficar' + adjective means 'to become': ficar vermelho (turn red), ficar triste (become sad), ficar bravo (get angry).

target: Eu tô na correria hoje.
tip: Tô is casual shorthand for estou: Eu tô na correria = I'm in a rush. Spoken, not written.

target: Ele é um cara muito simpático.
tip: 'Simpático' means nice or friendly, not English sympathetic; that sense is 'compreensivo'.

target: Ela é muito inteligente e dedicada.
tip: Two adjectives with 'e' (and): both must agree with the subject. 'Inteligente' is the same for both genders.

target: Ela é muito responsável e organizada.
tip: Adjectives ending in a consonant like 'responsável' don't change for gender; only 'organizada' shows the feminine -a.

target: Os irmãos dele são completamente diferentes.
tip: 'Dele' is 'de' + 'ele' = 'his'. Portuguese often marks possession this way: 'os irmãos dele' = his siblings.

target: Ela é morena de cabelos cacheados.
tip: In Brazil, 'morena' is a broad term that can mean brunette, olive-skinned, or dark-haired. It's used much more widely than in other Portuguese-speaking countries.

target: Os avós dela são super ativos.
tip: 'Avós' (plural) covers both grandparents together; the singular 'avô' is grandfather and 'avó' grandmother, split by the accent.

target: Tô a fim de comer pizza.
english: I'm in the mood for pizza.
tip: 'Estar a fim de' means 'to feel like' or 'to be in the mood for.' Casual but very common in everyday Brazilian speech.

target: Olha só, que coincidência!
english: Look at that, what a coincidence!
tip: 'Olha só' is a very common conversation opener meaning 'look' or 'check this out.' Used to draw attention to something.

target: De nada, foi um prazer.
english: You're welcome, it was a pleasure.
tip: 'Ir' and 'ser' share the same preterite forms: fui, foi, fomos, foram – context tells you which verb it is.

target: A praia estava vazia e tranquila.
english: The beach was empty and peaceful.
tip: Two adjectives: 'vazia e tranquila' – both feminine to match 'praia.' Masc. would be 'vazio e tranquilo.'

target: O trânsito está cada vez pior.
tip: 'Cada vez + comparative' means 'more and more' or 'increasingly': cada vez pior (worse and worse), cada vez melhor (better and better).

target: Ela ficou brava com a situação.
english: She got angry about the situation.
tip: 'Bravo/brava' in Brazil means angry (not brave). This is a common false friend – 'corajoso' means brave.

target: Que chato, choveu o dia inteiro.
english: How annoying, it rained all day.
tip: Que + an adjective or noun means how or what a: que chato (how annoying), que legal (how cool).

target: Eu esqueci de comprar o pão.
english: I forgot to buy the bread.
tip: Portuguese puts 'de' before the infinitive where English says forget to, so it is 'esqueci de comprar', not esqueci comprar.

target: Ele é menos tímido do que parece.
english: He's less shy than he seems.
tip: 'Menos... do que' is the comparison of inferiority: 'menos tímido do que' = less shy than.

target: As respostas dele foram curtas e grossas.
tip: 'Curto e grosso' is a set phrase for blunt or curt: 'respostas curtas e grossas' = short, blunt answers.

target: Os dias estão mais curtos no inverno.
english: The days are shorter in winter.
tip: Changeable, seasonal states use 'estar': 'os dias estão mais curtos' means the days are shorter now, not a fixed trait.

target: Meu chefe é mais novo do que eu.
english: My boss is younger than me.
tip: For people, 'mais novo' means younger, not 'newer'; the opposite is 'mais velho' (older).
